titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The angel's dream; the border crossed; Castejón surprised and the Henares raided (tiradas 19–23, lines 404–492)
part: Tiradas 19–23 · The angel's dream; the border crossed; Castejón surprised and the Henares raided (lines 404–492)

sentences.t:
I se echava mio Çid después que [fo de noch],
un sueñol priso dulçe, tan bien se adurmió.
sentences.l:
There himself-laid-down my Çid after that [it-was of night],
a sleep-to-him took sweet, so well himself he-fell-asleep.
sentences.i: There my Çid lay down once night had fallen; a sweet sleep took him, so soundly did he fall asleep.
sentences.n: Tirada 19 (assonance ó) — the angel Gabriel comes to the Çid in a dream. The line-endings carry a stressed ó (noch, adurmió, visión, Campeador, varón, to, santigó); a new assonance means a new tirada. This is the night at La Figueruela, where he went to lodge at v. 402. I = 'there' (Latin ibi), not 'and'. se echava, 'lay down'. The whole close of the line, [fo de noch], is Pidal's restoration (brackets = his italics); fo = fue, 'it was', the older preterite. sueñol = sueño + l(e), the pronoun glued on: 'a sweet sleep took him'; priso is the strong preterite of prender, 'to take, seize'. sueño here is 'sleep'; at v. 412 it will be 'dream'. se adurmió, 'he fell asleep'.

sentences.t:
El ángel Gabriel a él vino en [visión]:
“Cavalgad, Çid, el buen Campeador,
ca nunqua en tan buen punto cavalgó varón;
mientra que visquiéredes bien se fará lo to.”
sentences.l:
The angel Gabriel to him came in [vision]:
“Ride, Çid, the good Campeador,
for never in so good a point rode man;
while that you-shall-live well itself will-do the thine.”
sentences.i: The angel Gabriel came to him in a vision: “Ride on, Çid, good Campeador, for never did man ride out at so good a moment; as long as you live, all that is yours will prosper.”
sentences.n: [visión] is Pidal's restoration. The angel's message is the formula of the Çid's good hour turned into prophecy: en tan buen punto, 'at so good a point (of time)', the auspicious moment, kin to en buen ora. Cavalgad, 'ride', the plural imperative of courtesy. nunqua = nunca; nunqua … varón, 'never … (any) man': with nunqua set first, no second negative is needed. mientra que = mientras. visquiéredes, future subjunctive of vivir, built on its old strong stem visc-. bien se fará lo to, literally 'what is yours will be done well', i.e. it will go well with all that is yours (Pidal: 'bien irá lo tuyo'); fará = hará (f- for modern h-). to = tuyo, 'thy': the angel slips from the courteous vos (cavalgad, visquiéredes) to the familiar thou, and the short form gives the ó of the assonance.

sentences.t: Quando despertó el Çid, la cara se santigó.
sentences.l: When awoke the Çid, the face himself he-crossed.
sentences.i: When the Çid awoke, he made the sign of the cross over his face.
sentences.n: se santigó la cara, 'crossed himself on the face', the sign of the cross traced over the face on waking from a vision. The next tirada opens by saying the same thing again in a new assonance (Sinava la cara): the poem often links tiradas by such repetition.

sentences.t:
Sinava la cara, a Dios se [fo] acomend[ar],
mucho era pagado del sueño que soñado a.
sentences.l:
He-signed the face, to God himself [he-went] to-commend,
much was pleased with-the dream that dreamt he-has.
sentences.i: He signed his face with the cross and commended himself to God; he was well content with the dream he had dreamt.
sentences.n: Tirada 20 (assonance á) — heartened by the dream, the Çid marches to the sierra of Miedes, the frontier. The endings are acomendar, a, cavalgar, más, posar, han. Sinava, 'he signed', imperfect of sinar (= signar), restating santigó of v. 410 to link the tiradas. se [fo] acomend[ar], 'went to commend himself', ir + infinitive as a plain past (as iva posar, v. 402): [fo] and the -ar ending, which gives the assonance, are Pidal's. pagado, 'pleased, content' (pagarse, as at v. 69). soñado a = ha soñado: aver + past participle, the auxiliary set last for the assonance and spelt without h. sueño is now 'dream'.

sentences.t:
Otro día mañana pienssan de cavalgar;
es dia a de plazo, sepades que non más.
sentences.l:
Other day morning they-think of riding;
it-is day there-is of term, may-you-know that not more.
sentences.i: Next morning they set out to ride: one day of the term is left — be sure of it — and no more.
sentences.n: Otro día mañana, 'the next day in the morning', and pienssan de cavalgar, pensar de + infinitive, 'set about riding': stock formulas (v. 394). v. 414 is hard, and its construction is not certain. The likeliest sense is 'there is (only) a day of the term': a = ha, impersonal aver 'there is'. That fits the count of days: three were left at v. 307, and nights at Cardeña, Spinaz de Can and La Figueruela have passed since, so on this reading it is the last day the king allowed for leaving his kingdom. sepades que non más, 'know that there is no more', the minstrel to his hearers (as at v. 307).

sentences.t:
A la sierra de Miedes ellos ivan posar,
de diestro [Atiença] las torres que moros las han.
sentences.l:
At the sierra of Miedes they went to-lodge,
on right [Atiença] the towers that Moors them have.
sentences.i: At the sierra of Miedes they went to make their halt, on the right hand of Atienza, of the towers the Moors hold.
sentences.n: Pidal moves v. 398 here, printing it after v. 415 and keeping its number. In the manuscript it stands among the places passed on leaving Castile (vv. 396–400); its de diestro, 'on the right', answers de siniestro at v. 397. Pidal's note takes the phrase of the Çid's position, not of the town's: Atienza lies on the left of one facing south, and de diestro means that the Çid is on the right of Atienza (so too at v. 397, by his note, the Çid passes on the left of San Esteban). The words alone could also mean 'with Atienza on the right'; the translation follows Pidal. Pidal's print order is followed. ivan posar, ir + infinitive as a past, 'went to lodge'. The sierra de Miedes is the range near Miedes, between Castile and the Moorish lands to the south; the identification of these places is likely, not certain. [Atiença] = Atienza, a fortress town; the name is wholly Pidal's restoration. que moros las han: las takes up las torres, 'which Moors hold them'. aver here means 'to hold, possess'.

sentences.t:
Aun era de día, non era puesto el sol,
mandó ve[e]r sus yentes mio Çid el Campeador:
sin las peonadas e omnes valientes que son,
notó trezientas lanças que todas tienen pendones.
sentences.l:
Still it-was of day, not was set the sun,
ordered to-see his peoples my Çid the Campeador:
without the foot-troops and men valiant that they-are,
he-noted three-hundred lances that all have pennons.
sentences.i: It was still day, the sun had not yet set, when my Çid the Campeador had his men mustered: leaving aside the foot-soldiers, valiant men as they are, he counted three hundred lances, every one with its pennon.
sentences.n: Tirada 21 (assonance ó) — the muster at the sierra. The endings are sol, Campeador, son, pendones: ó, with ó-e counting the same, as in tiradas 14 and 17. Aun = 'still, yet'. non era puesto el sol, 'the sun was not set', ser + participle. mandó ve[e]r, 'ordered to see', i.e. held a review; the second e, which makes the word two syllables, is Pidal's. yentes = gentes. peonadas, bodies of foot-soldiers (peón). e omnes valientes que son most likely praises those same footmen, 'valiant men as they are'; the e makes it read a little like a second group, so the exact sense is not certain. notó, 'counted, took note of'. Lances with pennons are mounted knights, counted by their pennons as at v. 16: the sixty of Burgos have become three hundred.

sentences.t:
“Temprano dat çevada, sí el Criador vos salue!
El qui quisiere comer; e qui no, cavalgue.
sentences.l:
“Early give barley, so the Creator you save!
He who may-wish to-eat; and who not, let-him-ride.
sentences.i: “Give the horses their barley early, so may the Creator save you! Whoever wants to eat, let him eat; and whoever does not, let him mount.
sentences.n: Tirada 22 (assonance á, with á-e) — the night crossing of the sierra out of Alfonso's land; the ambush laid at Castejón. The endings are salue, cavalgue, grand, quitar, podrá, man, andar, dar, trasnochar, an, far, nadi, dan, Fenares, trae: a stressed á, and an unstressed final -e or -i after it does not change the assonance (as in tirada 18). The Çid speaks without a verb of saying. dat = dad, imperative; çevada = cebada, barley, the horses' feed. sí, 'so' (Latin sic), in a wish: 'so may the Creator save you'. salue keeps the u for v (= salve). In v. 421 the first verb is left out, 'whoever wishes to eat (let him eat)'; quisiere is future subjunctive, qui = quien.

sentences.t:
Passaremos la sierra que fiera es e grand,
la tierra del rey Alfonso esta noch la podemos quitar.
Después qui nos buscare fallar nos podrá.”
sentences.l:
We-shall-cross the sierra which wild is and great,
the land of-the king Alfonso this night it we-can quit.
After who us may-seek to-find us he-will-be-able.”
sentences.i: We shall cross the sierra, wild as it is and high; this very night we can leave King Alfonso's land behind. After that, whoever comes looking for us can find us.”
sentences.n: fiera, 'wild, rugged'; grand = grande. la tierra … la podemos quitar: the object is set first and taken up again by la; quitar, 'to leave' (as at v. 392). So the term is kept: if v. 414 is read as the last day, he is out of the kingdom on it. buscare, future subjunctive. fallar nos podrá = nos podrá hallar (f- for h- again): the pronoun sits between infinitive and verb, as in the split future, though here podrá is simply the future of poder. A challenge: once over the border, let any pursuer come and find him.

sentences.t:
De noch passan la sierra, vinida es la man,
e por la loma ayuso pienssan de andar.
sentences.l:
By night they-cross the sierra, come is the morning,
and by the slope down they-think of travelling.
sentences.i: By night they cross the sierra; morning has come, and they make their way down the slope.
sentences.n: vinida es, 'has come', ser + participle with a verb of motion (as Exido es, v. 201). la man = la mañana, the short form, here giving the assonance. loma, a ridge or hillside; ayuso, 'down, downward' (Latin ad deorsum), the opposite of arriba. pienssan de andar, pensar de once more.

sentences.t:
En medio d’una montaña maravillosa e grand
fizo mio Çid posar e çevada dar.
sentences.l:
In middle of-a forest marvellous and great
made my Çid to-halt and barley to-give.
sentences.i: In the midst of a wondrous great forest my Çid had them halt and feed the horses.
sentences.n: montaña in Old Spanish is often wooded high country, 'forest', rather than a single mountain; maravillosa e grand is a doubled epithet. fizo = hizo, fazer + infinitive, 'made (them) halt'; posar as at v. 415. çevada dar, the object before the infinitive.

sentences.i: He told them all that he meant to march through the night; vassals so good take it to heart: their lord's command they are bound to carry out in full.
sentences.n: Díxoles, les glued on. querié, imperfect of querer (-ié for later -ía). trasnochar, 'to go through the night', a night march. vv. 430–431 are general praise of good vassals, in the present: por coraçón lo an, 'they have it at heart', they take it willingly. mandado, 'command'; so = su. han a far = han de hacer, aver a + infinitive for obligation (as a mover [h]a, v. 169); far = fazer. an and han are the same word in two spellings.

sentences.i: Before night falls they set out to ride: my Çid does it so that no one may get wind of it. They rode on through the night and gave themselves no rest.
sentences.n: anochesca, present subjunctive of anochecer after ante que. por tal … que, 'for this reason, that'. ventasse is most likely the imperfect subjunctive of ventar, 'to scent, get wind of', as a hound does; the word and its exact sense are not certain. [lo] is Pidal's. no … nadi is the double negative: 'that nobody should scent it' (nadi = nadie). The present faze followed by a past subjunctive is the poem's usual tense-mixing. Andidieron = anduvieron, old preterite of andar. vagar, 'leisure, rest'; que = 'for'.

sentences.t:
O dizen Castejón, el que es sobre Fenares,
mio Çid se echó en çelada con aquellos que él trae.
sentences.l:
Where they-call Castejón, the-one that is on Fenares,
my Çid himself cast in ambush with those that he brings.
sentences.i: At the place they call Castejón, the one that stands on the Henares, my Çid laid himself in ambush with the men he has with him.
sentences.n: O = 'where' (Latin ubi); dizen, 'they call it'. Castejón is most likely Castejón de Henares, a Moorish town on the river Henares; Fenares = Henares, f- for modern h- again. sobre, 'on, by' (as sobre Navas de Palos, v. 401); Pidal's note puts it on the left bank of the Henares. çelada, 'ambush': men hidden to fall on an enemy by surprise; se echó en çelada, 'lay down in ambush'. trae, present after the preterite: tense-mixing again. trae and Fenares are á-e.

sentences.t:
Toda la noche yace [Mio Çid] en çelada,
commo los consejava Álbar Fáñez Minaya:
“Ya Çid, en buen ora çinxiestes espada!
sentences.l:
All the night lies [my Çid] in ambush,
as them counselled Álbar Fáñez Minaya:
“O Çid, in good hour you-girded sword!
sentences.i: All night long my Çid lies in ambush, as Álvar Fáñez Minaya was counselling them: “O Çid, in a good hour you girded on your sword!
sentences.n: Tirada 23 (assonance á-a) — Minaya's plan; Castejón taken by surprise; the raid down the Henares to Alcalá. The endings are çelada, Minaya, espada, conpaña, algara, ganançia …; a final -ia after the stressed á counts as -a. The new tirada goes back over the ambush of v. 436 in the new assonance. [Mio Çid] is Pidal's restoration, printed with a capital. consejava, imperfect, 'was advising': the plan that follows is Minaya's. Ya, the vocative 'O' (v. 41). en buen ora çinxiestes espada, the honorific formula: 'in a good hour you girded on your sword'.

sentences.i: You, with a hundred of this company of ours — since we shall draw Castejón out into an ambush — are to stay there and hold the rear; give me two hundred to go raiding; with God and your good fortune we shall take great spoils.”
sentences.n: The last three lines of this unit and the first of the next (441b–441e) are not in the manuscript: they are Pidal's restoration, printed wholly in italics and without numbers of their own. The letters b–e after 441 are ours, as with 181b–d, so that the traditional count stays undisturbed. The restored lines state the plan — a hundred to hold Castejón, two hundred to raid — that the Çid's answer from v. 442 takes up. aquesta = esta. sacar a çelada, 'to draw out by ambush'. fincaredes, 'you will stay' (fincar, f- for h-). la çaga (Arabic sāqa), 'the rear', here the force left behind to hold a base. dedes, present subjunctive of dar; pora = para. algara (Arabic al-ghāra, 'the raid'), a mounted plundering foray; ir en algara, 'go raiding'. auze, 'luck, fortune': a word of augury, usually traced to Latin avis, 'bird' (bird omens, v. 11); the word is rare and its exact sense not certain. feremos = haremos; ganançia here is booty.

sentences.t:
Dixo el Campeador: “bien fablastes, Minaya;
vos con los dozientos id vos en algara;
sentences.l:
Said the Campeador: “well you-spoke, Minaya;
you with the two-hundred go yourselves in raid;
sentences.i: The Campeador said: “You have spoken well, Minaya: you, with the two hundred, go off on the raid;
sentences.n: v. 441e is the last of Pidal's restored lines; with v. 442 the manuscript resumes, the Çid taking up Minaya's own words. fablastes, preterite, 'you spoke'. id vos = idos, 'go off': ir with the reflexive.

sentences.t:
allá vaya Álbar Á[l]barez e Álbar Salvadórez sin falla,
e Galín Garcia[z], una fardida lança,
cavalleros buenos que acompañen a Minaya.
sentences.l:
there let-go Álbar Á[l]barez and Álbar Salvadórez without fail,
and Galín Garcia[z], a bold lance,
knights good that may-accompany Minaya.
sentences.i: let Álvar Álvarez go with you, and Álvar Salvadórez, without fail, and Galín García, a bold lance — good knights to ride with Minaya.
sentences.n: Three of the Çid's knights named for the first time: Álvar Álvarez, Álvar Salvadórez and Galín García. The l of Á[l]barez and the z of Garcia[z] are Pidal's. vaya is a subjunctive of command; acompañen, in the relative clause, a subjunctive of purpose. sin falla, 'without fail', a filler for the hemistich. una fardida lança, 'a bold lance' (fardido = ardido, 'daring'): Martín Antolínez was called ardida lança at v. 79.

sentences.t: Aosadas corred, que por miedo non dexedes nada.
sentences.l: Boldly run, that for fear not you-leave nothing.
sentences.i: Ride boldly, and leave nothing behind for fear.
sentences.n: Aosadas, 'boldly, confidently' (osar, 'to dare'). correr, 'to run', is also 'to overrun, raid' a country. que … non dexedes nada, 'so that you leave nothing': non … nada is the double negative.

sentences.t:
Fita ayuso e por Guadalfajara,
fata Alcalá lleguen las algaras,
e bien acojan todas las ganançias,
que por miedo de los moros non dexen nada.
sentences.l:
Fita down and by Guadalfajara,
as-far-as Alcalá let-reach the raids,
and well let-them-gather all the gains,
that for fear of the Moors not they-leave nothing.
sentences.i: Down from Hita and by Guadalajara, let the raiders go as far as Alcalá, and let them gather up all the spoils, leaving nothing behind for fear of the Moors.
sentences.n: The raid runs down the valley of the Henares: Fita = Hita, Guadalfajara = Guadalajara, Alcalá = Alcalá de Henares. These identifications are likely, not certain. Fita ayuso, 'down from Hita'. The spelling Guadalfajara is as printed; its f most likely stands for the Arabic ḥ of the name (wādī al-ḥijāra, 'river of stones'), but this is not certain. fata = hasta. las algaras is now the raiding parties themselves. acojan, 'gather in'. non … nada again.

sentences.t:
E yo con lo[s] çiento aquí fincaré en la çaga,
terné yo Castejón don abremos grand enpara.
sentences.l:
And I with the hundred here will-remain in the rear,
will-hold I Castejón whence we-shall-have great protection.
sentences.i: And I, with the hundred, shall stay here in the rear; I shall hold Castejón, which will give us a strong refuge.
sentences.n: lo[s], the s Pidal's. fincaré en la çaga, 'stay in the rear', holding the base. terné = tendré, future of tener with its consonants swapped (tenré > terné). don = donde, 'from where'. abremos = habremos. enpara = amparo, 'shelter, defence'.

sentences.i: If any trouble should befall you on the raid, send me word with all speed to the rear; of such a rescue all Spain will speak.”
sentences.n: cueta = cuita, 'distress, trouble'. f[o]re = fuere, future subjunctive of ser, the o Pidal's. fazedme mandado, 'send me word' (mandado, 'message'). privado, 'quickly' (v. 148). acorro, 'help, relief', the help the Çid will bring. España here is the whole peninsula, Christian and Moorish. The capital D after a semicolon is as printed.

sentences.t:
Nombrados son los que irán en el algara,
e los que con mio Çid fincarán en la çaga.
sentences.l:
Named are those who will-go in the raid,
and those who with my Çid will-remain in the rear.
sentences.i: Those who are to go on the raid are named, and those who are to stay with my Çid in the rear.
sentences.n: Nombrados son, ser + participle: the lists are drawn up. irán, fincarán, futures inside the past.

sentences.t:
Ya [cr]ieban los albores e vinie la mañana,
ixie el sol, Dios, qué fermoso apuntava!
sentences.l:
Now break the dawns and was-coming the morning,
was-coming-out the sun, God, how beautiful it-was-dawning!
sentences.i: Now the dawn is breaking and the morning coming on; the sun was rising — God, how fair it dawned!
sentences.n: [cr]ieban, 'they break', is the present of crebar (= quiebran): the stem creb- with its stressed e turned ie, and the ending -an of the present. It is not an imperfect, which would be crebavan. The cr is Pidal's restoration, as in [cr]ebar at v. 235; what the manuscript has there is not shown in this text. The present crieban beside the imperfects vinie, ixie is the poem's tense-mixing. los albores, 'the dawns', plural as at v. 235. vinie = venía; ixie = salía, the imperfect of exir. fermoso = hermoso (f- again); apuntava, 'was breaking, showing'. The minstrel's Dios, … ! breaks into the narrative.

sentences.t:
En Castejón todos se levantavan,
abren las puertas, de fuera salto davan,
por ver sus lavores e todas sus hereda[nças].
sentences.l:
In Castejón all themselves were-raising,
they-open the gates, out leap they-were-giving,
for to-see their labours and all their inherit[ances].
sentences.i: In Castejón everyone was getting up; they open the gates and went pouring out to see to their tilled fields and all their lands.
sentences.n: se levantavan, 'were getting up'. abren, present between imperfects: tense-mixing. de fuera salto davan, 'they gave a leap outside', they streamed out (dieron salto, v. 244). lavores = labores, field-work and the ploughed land. hereda[nças], 'inherited holdings, lands', its ending restored by Pidal.

sentences.i: They have all gone out and left the gates standing open, with only a few people who had stayed in Castejón; the folk outside are all scattered over the fields.
sentences.n: son exidos, 'have gone out', ser with a verb of motion; an dexadas, 'have left', aver with the participle agreeing with las puertas. pocas de gentes, 'few of people', with partitive de. fincar[a]n, 'had stayed', the -ara form (from the Latin pluperfect), most likely with pluperfect force here, though it can also be a plain past; the a is Pidal's, and with it the line keeps the á-a assonance. gentes and yentes are one word in two spellings. derramadas, 'spread about, scattered'.

sentences.t:
El Campeador salió de la çelada,
[en derredor] corríe a Castejón sin falla.
sentences.l:
The Campeador went-out from the ambush,
[round about] he-was-running Castejón without fail.
sentences.i: The Campeador broke out of his ambush and raided all round Castejón.
sentences.n: salió de la çelada, 'came out of the ambush'. [en derredor], 'round about', is Pidal's restoration. corríe = corría, correr in its sense 'to raid, overrun' (v. 445); a Castejón, the place as direct object, with a. sin falla, the filler again.

sentences.t:
Moros e moras avienlos de ganançia,
e essos gañados quantos en derredor andan.
sentences.l:
Moors and Moorish-women they-had-them of gain,
and those flocks as-many-as round-about go.
sentences.i: Moors, men and women, they took as booty, and all the herds that were grazing round about.
sentences.n: avienlos = avíen + los, 'they had them', aver 'to get, hold'; de ganançia, 'as booty'. The captured people are counted with the cattle: captives were sold or held for ransom. essos, 'those'. gañados = ganados, 'livestock', with ñ as printed; quantos … andan, 'as many as go about', grazing.

sentences.i: My Çid don Rodrigo made straight for the gate; those who held it, when they saw the sudden attack, took fright, and it was left undefended.
sentences.n: adeliñava, 'was heading straight' (from liño, 'line'). vi[d]ieron = vieron, the older form with d, restored by Pidal. rebata, 'surprise attack, alarm'. ovieron miedo, 'they had fear'. f[o] dese[n]parada = fue desamparada, 'was abandoned', the subject la puerta understood; the o and the n are Pidal's.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid Ruy Díaz por las puertas entrava,
en mano trae desnuda el espada,
quinze moros matava de los que alcançava.
sentences.l:
My Çid Ruy Díaz through the gates was-entering,
in hand he-brings naked the sword,
fifteen Moors he-was-killing of those that he-was-overtaking.
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz rode in through the gates, his naked sword in his hand, and slew fifteen of the Moors he overtook.
sentences.n: The hero's names shift line by line: el Campeador (v. 464), mio Çid don Rodrigo (v. 467), mio Çid Ruy Díaz (v. 470). entrava, trae, matava: imperfect, present, imperfect, tense-mixing. el espada, the old article el before a feminine noun beginning with e-. alcançava, 'was overtaking'.

sentences.t: Gañó a Castejón e el oro y ela plata.
sentences.l: He-won Castejón and the gold and the silver.
sentences.i: He won Castejón, and its gold and its silver.
sentences.n: Gañó = ganó, spelt with ñ like gañados. a before the place-name as direct object (as a Castejón, v. 464b). ela = la, an archaic form of the feminine article (Latin illa); Pidal's note says he admits it here from a correction in the manuscript made in Per Abbat's own time.

sentences.t:
Sos cavalleros llegan con la ganançia,
déxanla a mio Çid, todo esto non preçia’ nada.
sentences.l:
His knights arrive with the gain,
they-leave-it to my Çid, all this not they-prize nothing.
sentences.i: His knights come in with the spoils and leave them with my Çid; they make nothing of it all.
sentences.n: Sos = sus. déxanla, la = la ganançia, 'they leave it to my Çid': the booty goes to the lord for sharing out. Pidal's apostrophe in preçia' marks a shortened form: his note explains it as preçian, its n merged with the n of nada, 'they prize (it at) nothing'. The verb is plural, so the subject is the knights, who make nothing of all this booty; why they make nothing of it the line does not say, and its exact force is not certain. non … nada, double negative.

sentences.i: And here are the two hundred and three out on the raid, riding without fear and plundering the whole land; Minaya's banner reached as far as Alcalá, and from there they turn back with the spoils, up the Henares and by Guadalajara.
sentences.n: Afevos, 'behold', the minstrel's pointing word (v. 262). los dozientos [e] tres: most likely the two hundred plus three of the named knights, but how the count is made is not stated; [e] is Pidal's. sin dubda: dubdar in Old Spanish also means 'to fear', so most likely 'without fear' here, though 'without doubt, surely' is also possible. The second half of v. 477, [toda la tierra preavan], is wholly Pidal's restoration; preavan, 'were plundering': Pidal supplies the verb prear (Latin praedare, 'to plunder'), which the poet uses at vv. 903, 913 and 937; prea = presa, 'booty'. The seña is Minaya's banner, the mark of his command. desí = desde allí, 'from there'. arriba, 'up', upstream, against ayuso at v. 446: the raid goes down the river and comes back up it.

sentences.t:
Tanto traen las grandes ganançias,
muchos gañados de ovejas e de vacas
e de ropas e de otras riquizas largas.
sentences.l:
So-much they-bring the great gains,
many goods of sheep and of cows
and of clothes and of other riches abundant.
sentences.i: Such great spoils they bring: much wealth in sheep and in cows, in clothing and in other riches in plenty.
sentences.n: Tanto, 'so much', exclamatory. gañados (= ganados): Pidal's note says the word is used broadly here, not only of herds but of clothing and all movable wealth, so that de ovejas e de vacas e de ropas … all hang on it, 'goods in sheep and cows and clothing'. ropas, clothing and cloth, goods of real value. riquizas = riquezas; largas, 'ample, abundant'.

sentences.t:
Derecha viene la seña de Minaya;
non osa ninguno dar salto a la çaga.
sentences.l:
Straight comes the banner of Minaya;
not dares none to-give leap at the rear.
sentences.i: Minaya's banner comes straight on; no one dares fall upon their rear.
sentences.n: Derecha, agreeing with la seña, 'straight on'. dar salto a, 'leap upon, attack' (at v. 459, salto davan, the same phrase meant 'rushed out'). la çaga here is the rear of Minaya's column. non … ninguno, double negative.

sentences.t:
Con aqueste aver tornan se essa conpaña;
fellos en Castejón, o el Campeador estava.
sentences.l:
With this wealth turn themselves that company;
behold-them in Castejón, where the Campeador was.
sentences.i: With these riches that company turns back, and there they are at Castejón, where the Campeador was.
sentences.n: aver here is a noun, 'goods, wealth' (the infinitive 'to have' used as 'what one has'). aqueste = este. tornan se, printed apart. fellos = fe + los, 'here they are' (= helos): the presentative fe, as in afé, Afevos (v. 476). o = 'where' (v. 435).

sentences.t:
El castiello dexó en so poder, el Campeador cavalga.
Saliólos reçebir con esta su mesnada,
los braços abiertos reçibe a Minaya:
sentences.l:
The castle he-left in his power, the Campeador rides.
He-went-out-them to-receive with this his household,
the arms open he-receives Minaya:
sentences.i: Leaving the castle held in his name, the Campeador mounts. He rode out to receive them with this household of his, and with open arms he welcomes Minaya:
sentences.n: dexó en so poder, 'left in his power', i.e. securely held by his own men. Saliólos reçebir = salió a recibirlos, a verb of motion with a bare infinitive (as reçebir los sale, v. 297). mesnada, a lord's household troop, the men who live and fight under him. esta su mesnada, demonstrative + possessive, like article + possessive (las sus bocas). los braços abiertos, 'with arms open', a phrase without a preposition.

sentences.t:
“¿Venides, Albarfáñez, una fardida lança!
Do yo vos enbiás bien abría tal esperança.
sentences.l:
“Come-you, Albarfáñez, a bold lance!
Where I you should-send well I-would-have such hope.
sentences.i: “You are come, Álvar Fáñez, bold lance that you are! Wherever I might send you, I would have just such hopes of you.
sentences.n: Pidal's punctuation ¿ … ! marks a greeting that is half question, half exclamation, as at v. 204 (Pidal's note calls it a question of greeting); the shading is uncertain. Albarfáñez, printed as one word. fardida lança, as at v. 443b. enbiás is most likely a shortened imperfect subjunctive (= enbiasse, enviase, like pudies, v. 309): 'wherever I should send you'. The form and the exact turn of the line are not certain. abría = habría, conditional of aver. tal esperança, 'such hope', of such an outcome.

sentences.t:
Esso con esto sea ajuntado, [e de toda la ganançia]
dovos la quinta, si la quisiéredes, Minaya.”
sentences.l:
That with this let-it-be joined, [and of all the gain]
I-give-you the fifth, if it you-should-wish, Minaya.”
sentences.i: Let that be put together with this, and of all the spoils I give you the fifth, if you will have it, Minaya.”
sentences.n: Esso con esto: what Minaya brings, together with what was taken at Castejón. [e de toda la ganançia] is Pidal's restoration. la quinta, the fifth: Pidal's note, from the Fuero de Cuenca, says that those who went on a raid received the fifth of what they took; the Çid's generosity lies in offering Minaya the fifth of the Castejón booty as well, which was due to the Çid as captain. dovos = do + vos; do = doy. si la quisiéredes, future subjunctive: a courteous 'if you will have it'.
